control_results.score_rationale: The policy clearly designates qualified individuals (CIO, CISO, ISSM, ISSO) responsible for overseeing the information security program with explicit roles and authority, but lacks detailed evidence regarding their expertise and the resources provided to them.
evidence: The ED CIO is the designated Senior Accountable Official for IT Risk Management. The CIO is the person formally authorized to assume responsibility for operating a system at an acceptable level of risk.
Designates a senior ED Information Security Officer to develop and maintain an agency-wide ISP in accordance with FISMA 2014, and carries out the CIO’s responsibilities for the ISP.

The ISSM supports the ED CISO in the execution of ED’s ISP. The ISSM serves as the liaison and primary point of contact and coordination between PO personnel responsible for cybersecurity activities and the ED CISO for IT security matters.
Each information system will be assigned at least one ISSO.
Develops and maintains an ED-wide information security program
gaps: The policy does not explicitly describe the process for validating the 'qualified' status of designated individuals (e.g., expertise, credentials).
Insufficient detail regarding the specific resources and authority granted to the designated qualified individual.
No requirements for ongoing professional development or evidence that the designated individual has sufficient expertise.
No explicit monitoring or metrics for effectiveness of the role.
recommendations: Add language specifying qualification requirements (e.g., necessary certifications, experience) for designated individuals responsible for information security.
Establish criteria and processes to ensure designated individuals receive appropriate authority and resources to implement and enforce the security program.
Require ongoing professional development and training for designated individuals to ensure expertise is maintained.
Define metrics and monitoring processes to assess the effectiveness and accountability of the qualified individual overseeing the program.

control_results.score_rationale: The policy formally documents periodic risk assessment, implementation of safeguards, and employee training but lacks explicit detail on measurement, systematic monitoring, and defined accountability metrics for risk-based safeguard effectiveness and continuous improvement.
evidence: "conducts assessments of the risk and magnitude of the harm... at no less than every three years or when significant changes occur to the system/network;" (Excerpt 5)
"Ensures that system weaknesses are captured in the Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M)..." (Excerpt 5)
"Ensures that system users and support personnel receive the requisite security training;" (Excerpt 5)
"Ensures provision of adequate funding to implement the security requirements that fall within the management authority of the ISO;" (Excerpt 1)
"Ensures that all IT systems under their purview are configured in accordance with most recent ED and Federal system security configuration guidance..." (Excerpt 5)

"Maintains an up-to-date listing of the information systems and assets, and information (data) under their control and maintains awareness of the cybersecurity risk posture of each information system;" (Excerpt 3)

"Ensures, in coordination with CORs and acquisition personnel, that cybersecurity is addressed in all IT-related procurements and contracts through appropriate language in requirements documents;" (Excerpt 3)
"Limits connections to publicly accessible Federal websites and web services to approved secure protocols" (Excerpt 2)

"Identifies, tailors, documents, and implements information security and privacy-related functional requirements necessary to protect ED information, information systems, missions, and business processes;" (Excerpt 2)
gaps: No explicit references to measuring or monitoring safeguard effectiveness or performance metrics for risk controls.
Continuous improvement and integration of feedback into safeguard design not codified.
Response to and detection of attacks are only implicitly covered—not described as formal processes.
Detail on periodicity and contents of employee training is general, lacking specifics on how risk assessment drives training update.
Accountability and ownership for ongoing risk management actions beyond policy/process absent.
recommendations: Establish and document metrics to monitor the effectiveness of safeguards derived from risk assessment outcomes.
Implement and formalize processes for continuous improvement of safeguards based on monitoring results and incident response lessons learned.
Specify detection and response processes for cyber attacks as part of risk mitigation, including roles and escalation procedures.
Tie employee training content and frequency to identified risks from the risk assessment and document this linkage in policy.
Include clear statements on assignment of accountability for maintaining safeguards and continuous evaluation of risk-related controls.

control_results.score_rationale: The policy formally documents and defines access controls, role-based access, least privilege, and separation of duties. However, measuring, monitoring or integrating these controls with formal metrics and risk management processes is not evident.
evidence: "Limits information system access to authorized users, processes actions on behalf of authorized users, or devices (including other information systems);" (Excerpt 4, Page 22)
"Limits information system access to the types of transactions and functions that authorized users are permitted to execute;" (Excerpt 4, Page 22)
"Employs the principle of least privilege, including for specific security functions and privileged accounts;" (Excerpt 4, Page 22)

"Uses non-privileged accounts or roles when accessing non-security functions, and; Prevents non-privileged users from executing privileged functions and audit the execution of such function." (Excerpt 4, Page 22)
"Reinforces the concept of separation of duties by ensuring that no single individual has control of any critical process in its entirety per NIST SP 800-53 (as amended);" (Excerpt 4, Page 22)
"Responsibilities for all privileged users must include... sufficient access rights to modify, including disabling, controls that are in place to protect the system." (Excerpt 1 and 3, Page 23)
gaps: No explicit reference to ongoing monitoring or measurement of access control effectiveness.
No defined metrics or accountability structures directly tied to access control compliance.
Limited detail on how role definitions are formalized and reviewed (RBAC maintenance process).
No evidence of continuous risk-based evaluation or improvement of access control processes.
recommendations: Establish metrics and regular reporting for access control effectiveness (e.g., number of failed access attempts, privileged account reviews).
Specify processes for periodic review and update of user roles and access permissions.
Integrate access control monitoring with risk management and incident response processes.
Identify ownership/accountability for maintaining, reviewing, and improving access controls.
Document a process for continuous improvement (e.g., lessons-learned-based updates) of access controls.

control_results.score_rationale: The policy clearly requires maintaining up-to-date inventories of systems and assets, assignment of responsibilities, continuous monitoring, and system security categorization, which collectively address inventory and the basis for classification. However, there is no explicit requirement or documented process mandating classification of data by sensitivity or a formal data inventory catalog specifically mapping locations of customer information.
evidence: Maintains an up-to-date listing of the information systems and assets, and information (data) under their control and maintains awareness of the cybersecurity risk posture of each information system;

Ensures current system inventories, system-level security plans, security reviews, corrective action plans, security authorization packages, and similar cybersecurity documents are developed, maintained, and posted to ED’s system of record for FISMA reporting.
Signs off that system security designations are appropriately determined prior to system acquisition/procurement in accordance with FIPS 199 security categorization;
Ensures NIST SP 800-53 (as amended) controls are appropriate to the system based on the FIPS 199 security categorization;
gaps: No explicit mention of cataloging all locations where customer information is stored, transmitted, or processed.
Lacks a formal data classification scheme that assigns sensitivity levels directly to data types or records.
Does not establish a process or methodology for performing data classification or mapping based on sensitivity across systems.
recommendations: Establish a policy section that explicitly mandates maintaining a comprehensive data inventory cataloging all locations (including applications, databases, endpoints, and third-party locations) where customer information is stored, processed, or transmitted.
Implement a formal data classification policy specifying sensitivity levels (e.g., public, internal, confidential, restricted) and the process for labeling data accordingly.
Define responsibilities and periodic review intervals for updating both the data inventory and classification in alignment with regulatory and business needs.
Integrate data classification requirements into risk management and access control processes.

control_results.score_rationale: The policy references the use of secure protocols (like TLS) and mandates compliance with NIST and FIPS standards, indicating intent to use industry-standard encryption. However, there is no explicit mention of encryption requirements for customer data at rest and in transit or of a defined key management process.
evidence: Limits connections to publicly accessible Federal websites and web services to approved secure protocols.
NIST SP 800-53 Revision 4, Recommended Security Controls for Federal Information Systems, including updates as of 1/15/2014, 2013
FIPS PUB 140-2, Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules
gaps: No explicit requirement to encrypt customer information both at rest and in transit.
No defined or described key management process.
Does not specify what constitutes industry-standard encryption within the policy body.
Does not clearly assign accountability or metrics for encryption requirements.
recommendations: Explicitly require encryption of customer information both at rest and in transit within policy language, referencing industry standards such as AES and TLS.
Establish and document a key management process aligned with FIPS 140-2 and NIST guidelines.
Define what constitutes industry-standard encryption in the policy for all relevant data types.
Assign clear accountability for encryption implementation and monitoring, and specify periodic effectiveness reviews.

control_results.score_rationale: The policy documents reference secure development practices and ongoing vulnerability management in general terms, but lack specific, formalized requirements for secure software development lifecycle (SDLC), security testing, and vulnerability remediation for in-house developed applications.
evidence: b) Ensures the requirements are effectively integrated into IT component products and information systems through purposeful security architecting, design, development, and configuration, following the ED change management processes; (Excerpt 1)

e) Ensures continuous monitoring of the information system’s security is performed and validates the information system against the System Security Plan (SSP) while managing and controlling any information system updates; (Excerpt 4)
f) Ensures that security patches for all assigned information systems are installed within the timeframe identified by ED policy; (Excerpt 4)
l) Ensures NIST SP 800-53 (as amended) controls are appropriate to the system based on the FIPS 199 security categorization; (Excerpt 4)
gaps: No documented policy specifically addressing secure coding standards or secure SDLC phases.
No explicit requirement for security testing (e.g., code review, penetration testing) of applications prior to release.
No detailed procedures for ongoing identification, triage, and remediation of application vulnerabilities.
Does not discuss integration of security in agile/DevOps or specific assignment of accountability for secure development.
recommendations: Establish a formal secure software development lifecycle (SDLC) policy that mandates use of secure coding standards (e.g., OWASP, static/dynamic analysis).
Require that all in-house applications undergo defined security testing (e.g., static analysis, penetration testing, code reviews) prior to deployment and periodically thereafter.
Document a process for ongoing vulnerability management specific to application development, including timely remediation and tracking.
Assign clear responsibilities for secure development activities and require training for developers on secure coding practices.
Integrate security requirements into procurement and development checklists, and establish metrics to monitor compliance with secure development practices.

control_results.score_rationale: The policy references federal and NIST guidance related to identity management and cites the use of PIV-based approaches, but it does not explicitly mandate multifactor authentication for all users accessing customer information systems or describe an approval process for alternative controls.
evidence: • NIST SP 800-63 Rev 3, Digital Identity Guidelines
d) Ensures automated information security and privacy capabilities are integrated and deployed as required and use PIV based approaches wherever possible; (Excerpt 5)

l) Ensures that all IT systems under their purview are configured in accordance with most recent ED and Federal system security configuration guidance, and Federal CIO Council guidance (e.g., OMB M-11-11 and the Federal Identity Credential and Access Management Roadmap and Implementation Guidance); (Excerpt 2)
gaps: No explicit statement requiring multifactor authentication for all individuals accessing information systems with customer information.
No defined or documented approval process for reasonably equivalent or stronger alternative controls if MFA is not used.
No mention of how exceptions or waivers are tracked, justified, or approved in writing by a qualified individual.
Lacks specific procedural detail for implementing, monitoring, or enforcing MFA.
recommendations: Update the policy to explicitly require multifactor authentication for all information system users accessing customer information.
Document a formal process for requesting, reviewing, and approving exceptions to MFA, including written approval by the qualified individual.
Define enforcement and monitoring mechanisms for MFA implementation and assign accountability.
Add requirements for periodic review of MFA effectiveness and continuous improvement aligned with risk management processes.

control_results.score_rationale: The policy acknowledges the need to protect information in all formats and references disposal, but lacks explicit, detailed procedures for secure disposal or concrete requirements for when and how customer information must be disposed. There is no evidence of a formal, documented process or monitoring mechanisms.
evidence: Provide adequate security for all information created, collected, processed, stored, transmitted, disseminated, or disposed of by or on behalf of the agency, to include Federal information residing in contractor information systems and networks.
The requirements of this Circular apply to management activities concerning all information resources in any medium (unless otherwise noted), including paper and electronic information.
gaps: No explicit policy requiring secure disposal procedures specifically for customer information.
No description of disposal methods (e.g., shredding paper, wiping digital media) or required standards.
No requirement for periodic review or assurance that information no longer needed is disposed of securely.
No mention of accountability, metrics, or monitoring of disposal activities.
No defined process or responsibility assignment for secure disposal across all media types.
recommendations: Develop formal, documented procedures for the secure disposal of customer information in all formats, including clear standards and methods.
Explicitly define triggers or review points for when information must be assessed for disposal.
Assign responsibility for secure disposal and require periodic audits to confirm compliance.
Integrate disposal activities with risk management and include monitoring or metrics to assess effectiveness.
Ensure agreements with service providers include secure disposal requirements for any customer information managed.

control_results.score_rationale: The policy includes formal, documented references to change management processes, major change reviews, and required notifications, but lacks detail regarding a thorough risk evaluation or consistent pre-implementation review requirements for all system changes.
evidence: "Ensures the requirements are effectively integrated into IT component products and information systems through purposeful security architecting, design, development, and configuration, following the ED change management processes;" (Excerpt 1)

"If a major change/upgrade to the system occurs, the documentation would require updating for the information system as required in ED’s selected central cybersecurity repository (currently CSAM);" (Excerpt 2)
"Notifies the ED CISO of any major changes to existing information systems or when planning the development of new information systems;" (Excerpt 4)
"Assesses the performance of security and privacy controls associated with the system/network or web service to ensure the residual risk is maintained within an acceptable range..." (Excerpt 5)
gaps: No explicit requirement for a thorough pre-implementation review for all changes, not just major ones.
Lacks defined processes or criteria to anticipate, assess, and document new risks created by all system changes.
No mention of how risk evaluations are integrated into the change management process or required sign-offs prior to implementation.
No clear metrics or monitoring of change management effectiveness described.
recommendations: Specify that all changes, not just major ones, require advance risk assessment and documented evaluation before implementation.
Define the process for anticipating and identifying new risks resulting from system or network changes.
Require formal pre-implementation reviews and sign-off steps that include risk analysis for customer information protection.
Integrate change management metrics and regular audits to assess process effectiveness and accountability.
Clarify roles responsible for conducting, documenting, and approving change-related risk assessments.

control_results.score_rationale: The policy mandates continuous monitoring, periodic FISMA reporting, annual security reviews, and vulnerability patch management, aligning with most of the control's requirements. However, it does not explicitly require annual penetration testing or biannual vulnerability assessments for all systems, and measurable metrics/accountability are not clearly established.
evidence: Ensures continuous monitoring of the information system’s security is performed and validates the information system against the System Security Plan (SSP) while managing and controlling any information system updates;
Ensures NIST SP 800-53 (as amended) controls are appropriate to the system based on the FIPS 199 security categorization;

Ensures that periodic FISMA formal performance measure metrics reporting (quarterly and annually) are completed on time and entered into ED’s selected central cybersecurity repository (currently CSAM);
Ensures system weaknesses, policy and standard deviations in the POA&M and entering them into the Department’s selected central cybersecurity repository (currently CSAM);
Conducts assessments of the risk and magnitude of the harm ... at no less than every three years or when significant changes occur to the system/network;
Ensures that actions are taken to respond and complies within specified timelines for any government-wide or ED-wide directed action items related to vulnerability patching;

control_results.score_rationale: The policy formally mandates information security and role-based training for all personnel, with supervisors responsible for enforcement and due dates, but lacks details on regular updates and measurement of training effectiveness.
evidence: Ensure personnel under their direct supervision complete all required information security training, including privacy and Role Based Training (RBT), within the mandated timeframe as needed.

gaps: No explicit mention of a defined schedule or process for regularly updating training content.

Implement procedures to assess and document the effectiveness of training programs (e.g., post-training tests, user feedback, tracking phishing simulations).
